messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Counselor
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 67

Sam is a 19-year-old counselor at a residential summer camp for teenagers recovering from serious medical conditions. He has been with his girlfriend, Maya, for just over a year. They moved in together three months ago, and Maya tells him he “still seems far away,” even when they’re in the same room.

He was 17 when he nearly died. It started as a headache that wouldn’t quit, then fever, then a stiffness in his neck that made it impossible to touch his chin to his chest. His mother drove him to the emergency room, and by the time they arrived he was disoriented, slurring his words. He remembers the harsh fluorescent lights, the cold metal of the stretcher, and a nurse’s voice saying “meningococcal meningitis” with a tone that meant serious. He remembers the spinal tap—the pressure, the slow dread of hearing the attending physician curse under his breath.

He spent twelve days in the ICU. The beeping of monitors, the hiss of the oxygen mask, the way his body felt like it was dissolving into the sheets. He remembers a chaplain visiting his room—someone he didn't ask for—and the look on his mother’s face when she thought he wasn’t watching. He was told later that his blood pressure had dropped so low they considered life support. He remembers none of that, only a blank, white silence like a dead channel on a TV.

When he finally came home, he was 40 pounds lighter and terrified of his own body. Every headache was the start of it again. Every fever, every stiff muscle, sent him into a spiral of frantic Google searches. He stopped going to school, stopped answering texts from friends. His girlfriend at the time broke up with him, saying he “wasn’t the same person.” He still carries that line in his chest like a splinter.

Now he works at the camp. He chose this job deliberately—wanted to turn his worst experience into something useful. He sits with kids who have had organ transplants, who lost limbs to cancer, who are learning to walk after strokes. He tells them they can get through it. He listens. He validates. He is good at his job. The parents say he’s a natural.

But at night, he lies awake next to Maya and tracks the rhythm of her breathing. If it gets too quiet, he shakes her gently until she stirs and says “what?” and he says “nothing, sorry, go back to sleep.” He cannot stand the thought of a body being still.

He avoids hospitals. He told his primary care doctor he’d follow up on a minor infection, but it’s been six months. The thought of walking past the automatic doors makes his mouth dry and his hands shake. Last week, a camper mentioned her brother was in the ICU with sepsis, and Sam had to leave the dining hall and sit in the parking lot, sweating, repeating “you are not in the hospital” under his breath until his heart slowed down.

He is hypervigilant about his own health. He checks his temperature three times a day, keeps aspirin in every bag, and once fainted in the grocery store after convincing himself the sore in his throat was a returning infection. Maya found him on the floor by the frozen foods, clutching his neck.

Professionally, he is admired. But privately, he still feels like the 17-year-old boy in the hospital gown—helpless, untethered, waiting for someone to tell him he’ll be okay. He has not told Maya that when she touches his shoulders from behind, he sometimes flinches before he can stop himself. He has not told anyone that he still replays the chaplain’s face in his head, that sometimes he checks his own pulse mid-sentence, that he fears he has not really survived at all—only borrowed time from a body he can no longer trust.
